paras: The attempted lynching of the Rufus Buck gang took place in the Creek Nation, Indian Territory, in August 1895, when crowds of citizens at Okmulgee and Muskogee tried to take five captured men from the officers holding them in order to lynch them. The officers slipped away from both crowds and took the prisoners by train to the federal jail at Fort Smith, Arkansas, where a court later sentenced them to hang.

According to the Fort Smith Elevator, the gang began on July 28 by killing a Black deputy marshal at Okmulgee, John Garrett. Over about ten days the men were accused of robbing stores and travelers, shooting a Black boy, and assaulting several women, among them a Mrs. Rosette Wilson and a Mrs. Hasson.

Creek light horse police under Capt. Edmund Harry and deputy U.S. marshals overtook the men while they divided loot from a store robbery, and after a gunfight all but one surrendered. The capture was dated August 8 by the Checotah and Wagoner dispatches and August 9 by a Tulsa dispatch. From the first reports a lynching was expected: the Tulsa wire said citizens were pursuing the officers "with the intention of taking them away," and the Checotah wire said "lynching is talked of."

At Okmulgee, a mob "bent on lynching them" surrounded the officers, who escaped with their prisoners to Muskogee. A Kansas City report said two hundred men surrounded the Okmulgee jail before being "prevailed upon to let the law take its course"; a Muscogee dispatch put the crowd at five hundred. At Muskogee another mob, "with ropes and rifles," was waiting, but the officers were warned in time to lodge the men in jail. The town stayed "in an uproar all night" until the crowd quieted long enough for the posse to leave by train for Fort Smith. The Wagoner dispatch added that a party of Muskogee citizens had gone across country to Fort Gibson to stop the Missouri Pacific train and deal out "summary justice."
The Fort Smith Elevator said the officers were allowed to bring the men in alive once the citizens were assured they would be turned over to Judge Parker's court.

A Fort Smith dispatch of August 13 reported Rufus Buck, Samuel Samson, Meoa Judy [Meorna July], Lucky Davis and Albert Stake lodged in the United States jail there. On September 25 Judge Parker sentenced Buck, Sampson, July, Lucky Davis and Louie Davis to hang on October 31 for an assault on a "Mrs. Hastings" near Okmulgee. No arrest or prosecution of anyone in the crowds at Okmulgee or Muskogee appears in the coverage.

The story reached white papers across the country through three wire dispatches, beginning on August 10 with a Tulsa dispatch carried by the Sacramento Record-Union, the New York Sun and the Richmond Dispatch. A Checotah dispatch ran the same day in the Indianapolis Journal and the Salt Lake Herald, among others. The longer Wagoner dispatch followed on August 12 in the Savannah Morning News, the Birmingham Age-Herald and the New-York Tribune, among others.

Headlines such as "Lynch the Fiends," "Lynching Looked For" and "Lynching is Easier" treated a lynching as likely or deserved. The Birmingham Age-Herald titled its story "Death Too Good for Them," and the Savannah Morning News wrote that "Desperate Citizens Well Nigh Go Wild in the Effort to Lynch the Scoundrels." The Fort Smith Elevator, reprinted in the Mountain Echo, wrote that the citizens "would certainly have been justified in putting an end to the whole gang."

Racial labels shifted: the Tulsa wire spoke of "Creek negroes" and the Coconino Sun of "Creek and Negro Desperadoes," while the Wagoner wire called the men "Indians." The Checotah wire stressed that the women assaulted were "white." All of the coverage found comes from white papers; no report of the episode was found in the Black press.

The race of the prisoners is the main disagreement: the first wire called all five "negroes," while the Fort Smith reports, from where the men were tried, called them Uchee Indians with one Black man. The Wagoner wire also had Lucky Davis escaping, but the Fort Smith reports list him among those jailed.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of the Rufus Buck gang
bases: Crowds at Okmulgee and Muskogee surrounded officers and a jail to take and lynch five prisoners accused of murder and assault, and a third party set out to stop their train, but the officers kept them (A13, A4, A15).

Crowds of 200 to 500 men tried to seize the prisoners to lynch them for alleged murders and assaults, but no one was killed; the officers delivered all of them to the federal jail at Fort Smith (A4, A21, A13, A23).

Separate dispatches from Tulsa, Checotah, Muskogee via Kansas City, Wagoner and the Fort Smith Elevator agree that the prisoners were captured near Okmulgee and that crowds sought to lynch them (A2, A5, A4, A13, A24).

accounts.label: Tulsa wire (via St. Louis Chronicle)
accounts.gist: Light horse police, three marshals and citizens captured 'Rufus Black and four other Creek negroes' on Flat Rock creek while dividing loot from an Orcutt store; citizens pursued the officers intending to take the prisoners.

accounts.label: Checotah wire
accounts.gist: Four men were arrested after a fight in the Concharty mountains, accused of ravishing three white women; lynching was 'talked of' and a strong guard would be needed.

accounts.label: Muskogee reports (via Kansas City and Muscogee)
accounts.gist: Two hundred (or five hundred) men surrounded the Okmulgee jail wanting to lynch the five, but agreed to let the law take its course.

accounts.label: Wagoner wire
accounts.gist: A mob at Okmulgee surrounded the officers, who escaped to Muskogee; a second armed mob there kept the town in uproar all night; a third party went to intercept the train for Fort Smith.

accounts.label: Fort Smith Elevator
accounts.gist: Lynching was 'freely talked of', but on assurance the men would go to Judge Parker's court the officers were allowed to bring them in alive.

framing.detail: The Birmingham Age-Herald headed the Wagoner wire 'Death Too Good for Them', and the Savannah Morning News deck read 'Desperate Citizens Well Nigh Go Wild in the Effort to Lynch the Scoundrels'.
The Fort Smith Elevator wrote that the citizens 'would certainly have been justified in putting an end to the whole gang'.
Most papers ran one of three wires under headlines such as 'Lynch the Fiends', 'Lynching Looked For', 'Lynching is Easier' and 'Danger of a Lynching'.

versions.value: Uchee Indians except Lucky Davis, 'a negro'

conflicts.note: The Fort Smith reports, written where the men were jailed and tried, are the most specific; all versions describe at least one prisoner as Black.
The Checotah dispatch dated Aug. 9 says 'yesterday'; the Tulsa dispatch dated Aug. 9 says 'late this afternoon'.
The Fort Smith reports list Lucky Davis among the five jailed, supporting the Checotah and Elevator version.
Both reports come from Muskogee by wire; neither is local.
